Oral evidence - 18 Nov 2026

Transport Committee

Oral evidence: Road Safety Strategy, HC 81

Wednesday 18 November 2026

Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 18 November 2026.

Watch the meeting

Members present: Ruth Cadbury (Chair); Staff Aquarone; Dr Scott Arthur; Jacob Collier; Samantha Dixon; Daniel Francis; Olly Glover; Alex Mayer; Joe Morris.

Questions 218-251

Witnesses

I: Professor Siddartha Khastgir, Head of Safe Autonomy, Warwick Manufacturing Group, University of Warwick; Ashley Patton, Chief Engineer in Test Services, HORIBA MIRA; Stuart Lovett, Chair, TyreSafe; Professor Richard Cuerden, Academy Director, Transport Research Laboratory.

Written evidence from witnesses:

– Professor Siddartha Khastgir

– HORIBA MIRA

– TyreSafe

Examination of witnesses

Witnesses: Professor Siddartha Khastgir, Ashley Patton, Stuart Lovett and Professor Richard Cuerden.

Chair: Welcome to this morning’s evidence session, which is the penultimate oral session of our inquiry into the Government’s road safety strategy. We will be hosting two panels this morning. With our first panel we will focus on vehicle safety and the role of emerging technologies in improving road safety. In our second panel we will hear from road safety campaigners who have submitted written evidence to our inquiry, and who will draw on their lived experience of the issue.

Before we begin I remind witnesses and Committee members that we should not discuss specific cases if any legal proceedings on those cases are not completely finished. Please feel free to talk about the wider policy issues. Will our first panel of witnesses please introduce themselves, starting with Professor Siddartha Khastgir, who is joining us from India, so I guess it is good afternoon, or even good evening.

Professor Khastgir: It is good evening, actually, and I am in Japan right now. Thank you so much for the invitation; I am very grateful. I am a professor at WMG, University of Warwick and the head of safe autonomy. I am also a member of the Department for Transport’s Science Advisory Council. I would like to thank the Committee and the Chair for allowing a virtual link for this session.

Professor Cuerden: I am a director at the UK’s Transport Research Laboratory. My reason for being here is that I led the team that took the general safety regulation updates through the European Commission and the European Parliament to get systems, including ADAS, mandated.

Stuart Lovett: I am the chair of TyreSafe, a registered road safety charity.

Ashley Patton: I am chief test engineer at HORIBA MIRA UK. I am here to support the view in respect of the more practical implementation on the ground for the type approval of OEMs and with Euro NCAP.

Chair: What role do “safer vehicles” play in enabling the Government to deliver the KSI targets set out in the road safety strategy?

Professor Khastgir: The first important thing to highlight here is that all the road crashes that happen right now are preventable, and many can already be prevented through vehicle technologies. We have technologies such as advanced driver assistance systems, autonomous emergency braking, lane-keep assist and so on, which can be mandated as part of the regulations to ensure we can help meet the targets.

It is very important to highlight that all these vehicle technologies that we are introducing or want to introduce will only benefit and deliver the targets for us if we get users to use them. There is a big issue right now with all these vehicle technologies, in that a lot of users tend to switch them off or do not use them in the way they need to be used. While vehicle technologies have a big role to play in order to meet the targets, they will only play that role if we can ensure people use them and use them correctly.

Chair: We had an interesting discussion in my household with our new car.

Professor Cuerden: I agree with everything Siddartha said. If we accept the state of play today—let us say these systems are not being used as efficiently as they could—we estimate that the systems are preventing 14,000 from being killed or seriously injured. That is a cost-benefit ratio of 5:1. It has been really beneficial to introduce what we have now. Exactly as Siddartha was saying, what we have now could be so much better. That is the challenge for the rest of the conversation.

Stuart Lovett: I agree with my other panel members. Safer vehicles are absolutely crucial in delivering the road safety strategy. The issue here—certainly from TyreSafe’s point of view—is that as we have moved away from crash survivability to collision-avoidance systems, those systems that we are going to be relying on in the future for new vehicles and technology are compromised if people are driving around with an illegal or defective vehicle, particularly in respect of tyres and brakes.

Ashley Patton: Something we have to think about is how far other people go in safety standards. If you look at a GSR2 vehicle, which is exactly the 18 safety implementations we are looking at, that would be scored as a zero-star Euro NCAP car. The point for this really is that the majority of vehicles sold today already get an NCAP star, and usually five. That means that already the majority of manufacturers in unlimited series are going much further beyond what we have already in terms of GSR2.

Chair: Do you all agree that if the 18 safety technologies for new vehicles come in—as the Government are currently consulting on—the reported number of 14,000 prevented from death or serious injury is roughly correct and will achieve that level of drop?

Stuart Lovett: I accept that it will be a slow burn. If we consider that the average age of the vehicle fleet in this country is now 10 years, for any new vehicle coming on board we will miss the 2035 deadline for the casualty reduction targets. We have to remember that that 14,000 is over 15 years, which is less than 1,000 a year. We have to look at the current and existing fleet of vehicles in this country, which is in the evidence that we have submitted to the Committee. We need to consider the current state of vehicles in this country. What can be done—as Siddartha said—is raise awareness with the public that these are not complementary systems; they are essential in enabling the ADAS systems to work effectively and do their job.

Joe Morris: What are the main weaknesses in the current vehicles standards framework? What changes to the regime do you believe the Government should prioritise?

Professor Khastgir: First, if we adopt the GSR2 standards—as we all agree to—the only way this will deliver on the benefits is to ensure the performance of these technologies remains the same throughout life. That is a big challenge right now, because most of our MOT mechanisms do not look into the ADAS technologies or the sensor-based technology. There are a lot of reports right now in terms of sensor calibration being off, and as a result the systems are not performing like they were on day zero.

While we have the vehicle standards in terms of day-zero performance, the big, important aspect that we need to ensure is how we ensure the day-zero performance remains throughout life. That has to be done through an updated MOT regime and other aspects of ensuring a much more robust sensing capability, because all these 18 technologies will have lots of sensing capabilities.

Professor Cuerden: I am going to rattle off five points, because it is such a crux point of the conversation. First, it is essential in my mind that the 18 measures are adapted. We should think of them as the introduction level: this is what gets us started. What do I mean by that? We talk about these 14,000 killed and seriously injured.

Secondly, if we have the legislation in place, we can then look at ADAS. Siddartha talked very well at the beginning about the fact that not everybody uses it well—people turn it off. How do we then get intelligent speed assistance and similar measures so that their specifications are much tighter and they are intelligent about how they warn me? Let me give you an example: if I am driving along at 31 mph and the limit is 30 mph, perhaps I do not need all the alarms on the vehicle going off at the same time; if I am doing 50 mph in a 30 mph then I do need them. We could really improve how that is done.

My third point, which links to Siddartha’s point, is around bringing the MOT testing regime up to date. At the moment we know that for vehicles that are fitted with ADAS systems, the reliance is that they are working if there is a warning light on. Some self-diagnostic systems do not put that warning light on when they are not working.

You may ask the panel about headlight glare. We are taking on board the EU implementing directive for more traditional measures. With headlamp adjustment, if you adjust to the shoulder height of headlights you are going to have glare on the road on some vehicles, because it is really hard to make that work.

Fourthly is HMI, which I am sure my colleagues will talk more about. We now have screens in the vehicles. People talk about touch screens, and we like to talk about look screens. I used to reach and feel a button; I had haptic feedback. Now I have to look, take my eyes and brain off the road and find a menu. That whole HMI thing needs improving. The EU directive on this, which is not laid out in any specific requirement, says that the human-machine interface with a screen in a vehicle should be no worse than the 1990s vehicle with buttons. We have failed; we have made it worse.

My fifth and final point is a really serious one. We have seen really good progress—although there is much more to do—with protecting people in buses, cars and vans. We have been shamefully poor at protecting pedestrians and cyclists when they are struck by vehicles. We need to address that.

Stuart Lovett: The main thing for us is that the technology that is coming will be essential and of course we will support it, but the standards that are being talked about are, as I say, really for the future. They are not in most of the current fleet of cars out there—the 40 million vehicles on our roads. The MOT, which obviously we are happy to talk about in more detail, is really the only measure of vehicle condition.

What we are advocating for is having something in the strategy around the state of vehicles on our roads today. We are working closely with DVSA and the MOT testing team. By utilising that data can we not only predict where potential incidents may occur. It is also very good evidence of where people are not taking action, which will compromise the systems we are talking about by not acting when they have had an advisory from the MOT.

Most people are under the belief that if you pass the MOT then the vehicle is safe. We know that there is something in the order of 1.5 million vehicles that pass their MOT but have a safety-critical issue that can be ignored, which again can compromise the systems that we are talking about. If nine out of 10 of those safety-critical advisories are down to tyres and brakes, why are we not doing more to raise awareness around vehicle condition on our roads today?

Ashley Patton: If we look at some OEM strategy, it is putting safety behind a paywall feature. Is safety really an option? Let us consider that one. In terms of implementation, the safe system is important. If we think about intelligent speed assist, we need the signs to be legible, not covered in graffiti, turned the wrong way or just needing cleaning. It can be something very simple like that. Let us start with the basics—for example, white paint on the roads is very important for emergency lane-keeping systems. Starting with the basics is a really important point here.

The other thing is around systems working as we expect they should. At the moment OEMs have a different perspective on that, and we do not really have any level of guidance or real industry knowledge collectively about what a system should do. If we sit here and talk about false positives, there are some that are very obvious in terms of the system going off when it should not, to Richard’s point. On the ones where it is a bit more ambiguous, do we really know whether it should have warned you or not? We need research and funding for this.

In addition, if we talk about the way that information is displayed in HMI—again, as Richard said—even Euro NCAP has had to say that we need to bring back buttons because of OEMs putting in different ways to turn features off. For example, to turn fog lights off it can be under three or four menus on a touchscreen. You are already looking down so it is not safe by design.

We also have things such as mirroring for phones—for example, Apple CarPlay. If you go into some applications, you might have a sat nav in one and your vehicle says the speed is one limit; you look on your other screen and it is a completely different one. A vehicle with intelligent speed assist has to go through a regulatory process to confirm that what it is actually displaying is the right information, yet I can put whatever app I have downloaded, from wherever that has come, from whoever knows, on to the centre screen and it gives me a completely different speed. How is that okay?

Chair: I can recognise that.

Joe Morris: Mr Patton, in your written evidence you say that the legislation governing front and side protection has not changed substantially since 1994. What risks do you feel current safety tests are failing to capture?

Ashley Patton: We have used the same anthropomorphic devices—essentially the crash test dummies—in passive safety systems for a significant amount of time. If we look at what is happening in Euro NCAP, pushing the envelope of different representations of demographics, it is using females that are different sizes and children that are actually the size of children rather than just scaled-down adults. The information we can gather from these much more advanced devices helps us to optimise restraint systems to protect occupants to the optimal level. We have just had a recent advert from one OEM that is a world leader in this area, and it has started advertising the second generation of the safety seatbelt where it is now making the restraint system fit for all.

Professor Cuerden: That is a really good point. The European Commission—with some advice from experts such as ourselves—made the decision that it was too expensive and difficult to get a female crash test dummy developed and validated in time to be in regulation, because it would take 10 or 15 years. This means that up until the general safety regulation came in in Europe, we were protecting a 75 kilogram US Air Force male—that was the entry criteria.

What we chose to do with the general safety regulation was introduce a frontal overlap test that was already in NCAP and developed with the same dummies. By testing in different conditions we got the same benefits. The restraint system is now much kinder and softer, and we have more severe pulses for women and people like me who are getting a bit older. We have helped solve the problem but by doing it through a different route. Everything that Ashley said is true; we can do a lot more.

Dr Arthur: Ashley, you mentioned that some safety features are behind paywalls. Can you give an example of that?

Ashley Patton: If we look at higher levels of automation, they are typically a paywall subscription. Let us go to the more basic element: if you go and buy a car today from some OEMs, safety features are a standard fitment. You can tick the other box that says optional. Maybe there are builds of vehicles that are available on a special deal that do not have that optional feature; they are not going to have it.

Dr Arthur: Is that de-specifying? Rather than going further are you going lower?

Ashley Patton: We could look at the glass half full or half empty; it is de-specifying or up-specifying. The reality is you can buy a model of a vehicle with everything on it—let us say a five-star Euro NCAP—that is absolutely cutting-edge in safety technologies, and maybe a lower one without the safety pack will be different.

Dr Arthur: When you mentioned a paywall I assumed you meant software-based features so that you could somehow deactivate or have more control over the features within your touchscreen. Are you talking about the basic specification of the vehicle?

Ashley Patton: Essentially. This is a trend. Automotive competition is incredibly fierce. Coming out of a large OEM previously myself, we used to do value engineering and look at how we could reduce anything. We would remove a label on a plastic bag on a tyre inflator in the boot because it would save a tenth of a penny on each one. If there is an opportunity to reduce cost for competitive safety features in a software-defined vehicle—if it is not mandated through the leadership on the GB scheme—then there could potentially become a paywall. It is an industry trend.

Alex Mayer: The Prime Minister is keen to align more closely with the European Union. Since we have left there has been some divergence of British vehicle standards from EU ones. What are the road safety implications of that? In which areas do you think we should be aligning or perhaps going further?

Ashley Patton: There are other elements that I see within this—for example, micromobility. We are constantly seeing a change in environment, but even with safety systems we need to understand how micromobility devices are used to be able to potentially protect from them at a vehicle technology level. Until we know that they will, or should, only ever be on roads in flow of traffic, the way in which we get legislation on how they are to be used is going to be really important, because that can then help us to be potentially proactive in technologies rather than reactive.

Alex Mayer: I cannot imagine any Government suggesting that we have lots of e-scooters on the pavement, so surely you can get to work right now on the sense that they are going to be on the road, without waiting for Government.

Ashley Patton: Potentially. What is the motivation for an OEM to start looking at this if it is not actually legislated for? In theory they are illegal devices and other than the trials that are in city centres—

Alex Mayer: They are long-winded trials.

Ashley Patton: We have a lot to learn from European territories.

Stuart Lovett: I do not really have anything more to add on the technology and whether that complies with EU or global standards. From TyreSafe’s point of view obviously our concern around the state of the fleet now, and with the coming technology, is that the systems will be compromised if we have unsafe vehicles due to the vehicle condition itself.

Professor Cuerden: At the moment, until we get the legislation in place so that we have these 18 vehicle tech measures in Great Britain, we are behind the EU27, which has more stringent, mandatory requirements. Of course lots of vehicles sold today meet and surpass them already through Euro NCAP. Do you remember I talked earlier about this being the platform? If you have an advanced driver assistance system and ISA on the vehicle—or whatever it might be—we know we can improve upon and influence that standard if we are aligning with our friends, neighbours and international markets. We can help improve how the system performs; it will get better both in terms of it knowing to keep me in lane or at the right speed, but also in how it communicates with me. If we are not aligned with it, that comes in and we just accept it with the nature of the market.

Professor Khastgir: I agree with everything that has been said. I would like to add a specific point. Some new vehicle technologies are being regulated at the United Nations level. The European Commission, member states, the UK and other parts of the world are collaborating to do a joint regulation. While we are talking about GSR, and what Richard has said is very true, the new vehicle technologies—such as hands-off driver assistance systems and automated or autonomous emergency braking—are regulated at the United Nations level. By definition the UK is already adopting them because it is part of the UN regulation and we are a member of the 1958 agreement, which entails our adoption of those regulations.

Alex Mayer: Ashley, your written evidence recommends closer alignment with European regulatory standards. Which requirements that do not currently apply to British vehicles do you think should be prioritised?

Ashley Patton: It should be all 18. Let us not ignore alcohol interlock devices. They are a set of requirements on how to be able to meet a goal. In terms of other things that are happening in Euro NCAP, essentially it is saying that European regulations are the lowest level so we should adopt them.

Alex Mayer: What would the benefits be of aligning regulatory standards more closely with European new car assessment programme benchmarks?

Professor Cuerden: I started my career collecting the data that became Euro NCAP. Euro NCAP is amazing because it encourages innovation and it is fresh. Regulation takes time. We probably need to accept that there is a lead lag, so why do we not use consumer testing that can be more agile, act quickly, improve the standards and testing and get real change on the road, and then the regulation will catch up? That will be international, either through the UN or relations with our partners. Supporting Euro NCAP to be more innovative will be really key.

Stuart Lovett: To argue from TyreSafe’s view, what you have to remember is that a vehicle is always tested to get its star rating, and even its fuel performance is done on a test track with new tyres, very often pre-warmed, in dry conditions. The American Automobile Association has done some work on a test track; unfortunately we do not have anything comparable in terms of research, which is why one of our requests is for research around worn tyres. The highway code talks about 96 metres being the stopping distance in dry conditions when travelling at 70 mph. The AAA says a vehicle with a tyre tread that is down to 3 mm increases stopping distances by 43% in wet conditions. In the UK, the legal minimum tread depth is 1.6 mm, so 3 mm is still perfectly legal. When you think about the kinetic energy from the vehicle being transferred to the road surface, the state of the tyres will affect the stopping distances and the strategies relying on the ADAS systems to prevent collisions in the future by enabling autonomous stopping.

Professor Khastgir: In some cases the regulations are leading the Euro NCAP standards. For example, a lot of the work on hands-off driving for driver assistance systems at the United Nations already exists as a regulation, but Euro NCAP does not have a standard for that. My suggestion and request would be to adopt the best that exists. If the best is at Euro NCAP, adopt that. If the best is at the United Nations, adopt that. Ultimately, safety is what we want; we do not care if it comes from Euro NCAP or the United Nations.

Jacob Collier: Have the Government struck the right balance between safety technology in new vehicles and those that currently exist on the road?

Professor Cuerden: There is a challenge isn’t there? We want all our new vehicles to be increasingly safe, and of course they must be safe for their lifetime. I mentioned earlier in my five points that we do not yet have an MOT system that is keeping pace with vehicle technologies and changes. Based on what we are doing today it will be difficult to know, as a vehicle ages, how that vehicle is performing throughout its life, and that is a risk to us.

Stuart Lovett: I agree; it is a potential risk. Unfortunately the gap in the strategy is that we are not looking at this at the moment. It is something that could easily be rectified by using the Government’s own data and more evidence of what the MOT testing stations are saying.

Ashley Patton: There is quite a bit of research work going on in the private sector to start understanding this. For example, if you look at when you replace a windscreen, even the change in the thickness of the glue to which the camera bracket is attached could mean the camera is pointing in a completely different direction. On a self-check procedure it looks fine, but the reality is that the car thinks it is pointing in a completely different direction than it is. There is fledgling research here and some private sector companies are spending significant amounts, but support is needed.

Jacob Collier: Professor Siddartha, do you have anything to say about what the Government could do to correct that imbalance?

Professor Khastgir: Absolutely. I would like to give a statistic. An agency of the Department for Transport—the DVSA—published a report in October of this year where it found that from the five most popular cars that exist on UK roads, three did not pass every test of the UN regulation for autonomous emergency braking. This was randomly done in the vehicle lifetime, not on day zero. The Government absolutely can and should do more on the fact that it is not just okay to have these good safety technologies; it is equally important that we have a regime that ensures their performance throughout life.

Jacob Collier: Stuart, I want to pick up on your point about tyres. When I visited a business in my constituency, it was talking about the second-hand market, which is particularly prevalent now, and obviously we do not know the safety of those particular tyres. Do you feel that the Government are doing enough around this, and particularly the second-hand market?

Stuart Lovett: We need to confirm for Committee members that we call them part-worn tyres. As soon as you drive off in a brand new vehicle your tyres are second-hand. We are working increasingly with Trading Standards officers in relation to part-worn tyres. What we are detecting from going in and doing the inspections with the Trading Standards recently is that complacency is absolutely rife, even with the people selling the part-worn tyres you mentioned. Why should you be able to buy a safety-critical component for £10 when we know that roughly 100% are being sold illegally? They are not being tested properly and the people selling those tyres do not know what the standards are, what the law is or that they are selling them illegally.

We did some work with Norfolk county council Trading Standards. Out of 191 part-worn tyres that were inspected—after giving them six weeks’ warning that it was coming in to look at them—190 were illegal. We did some work with Dudley council, and five out of five retailers were selling tyres illegally and did not even realise it. The more we look at this, the more needs to be done. If you are saying to somebody at the moment, “Why would you buy a tyre for, say, £100 when you can buy a tyre that is £10?”, of course the consumer is going to think, “Well, if it’s being sold quite openly in the high street or down some side road then it must be okay,” but the evidence is absolutely clear that they are not.

TyreSafe’s position is that because they are legally available we do not lobby Government; we go with whatever the legislation is today. We are not saying too much other than that Trading Standards needs to make sure that those tyres that are available to the public are sold in a safe, legal and compliant manner, and they are not at this moment.

Chair: It is somewhat ironic that we are talking about safety when the building is falling apart around us. Luckily no one is hurt; maybe a little shocked.

Dr Arthur: On this issue of old versus new cars, when I got my first car—a Vauxhall Nova—it was five years old. A new car was safer than that. Why should we be concerned about this right now if it has always been the case?

Professor Cuerden: The MOT system was basically developed to make sure that the seatbelts would still work, the vehicle was not rusty, structurally it was sound, the brakes and tyres were in good condition and those sorts of things. That has not changed for a long time. When we saw the big casualty benefits that came in post-Euro NCAP on the front and side, it was because the structural crashworthiness of the vehicles improved—we protected people in them. We saw that the testing of the structures matched the vehicles developing, and that all worked well for quite a long time.

What has happened in the last 15 years is that we have introduced computers and technology to our vehicles. We talk about these technologies as if they are all the same. For example, we talk about autonomous emergency braking systems as if the one that was on the 2014 vehicle is the same as the one on the 2026 vehicle, but they are not. They are very different systems. They do the same thing: look forward, see a pedestrian or a vehicle and brake for you. But the way they perform—the kit and the software—is different. At the moment all we can do is ask, “Is the warning light that is self-diagnosing itself working? Yes or no.” That step change of going from a physical, mechanical evaluation of the vehicle to a digital evaluation is our challenge now.

Professor Khastgir: Another challenge that we are seeing is the fact that when you are buying a second-hand car right now you are not given an overview of how the vehicle systems—especially the intelligence system—work. When you are buying it off the showroom you get some level, albeit not great, of input on how to use the different adaptive cruise control and driver assistance systems. When you are buying a second-hand vehicle you do not get that, so you either end up not using it or using it incorrectly, which is a bigger issue that we did not have in the previous era of vehicles.

Dr Arthur: With my Vauxhall Nova it was much easier for me—even as a novice—to check that it was operating properly. Its only mod con was a clock inside the driver cabin; those were different times. We were talking earlier about the number of drivers who are switching these systems off. What is the solution to that? Do we pass legislation saying that people must use it? Do we link it into insurance, saying, “If you have a crash and you are not using it, your insurance could be void?” Do we just try to educate the public? I am not really aware of any Government public education programme actually working in this domain. What is the solution? It is easy to complain about people switching them off, but what do we do?

Professor Cuerden: The really interesting thing here is that there is a bit of bad press over this. Even if we said, “The EU is going to introduce speed limiters on everything,” if you look at the regulation, it is not. It is speed-limit information, and you can either warn the driver if they are over speed or otherwise control it.

Dr Arthur: That is a good example is it not? Why would my car let me drive over 100 mph in a 70 mph zone?

Professor Cuerden: With the media’s sensationalism about the vehicle taking control it is about the perception of whether people and the public are ready for that to happen. For the DFT, as a Euro NCAP member, there is a lot more we can do to disseminate resources from objective testing that exists on vehicles that are in unlimited series for the majority of cases. There is a lot more that we can do to help to educate.

Professor Siddartha just said that if you buy a used car they do not introduce what the vehicle will do with the safety features. From a lot of the experiences that I get, when you buy a new car they do not show you what to do with it other than how to switch it off. I would say to anybody in this room that you could go to five dealers and just say, “I know nothing about driver assistance systems; can you tell me something about them?”, and they will just say, “This is the off button and that’s how you turn it off. Every time you turn the car off you need to go and do it again.” The way in which we are presenting these—from a dealer level as well—is not particularly great and we have a bad reputation. That is one of the potential sources of this.

Dr Arthur: I have seen vehicles marketed on the fact that it is one button to switch it all off rather than having to switch things off independently.

Professor Cuerden: That is right: they are saying that that is a safety feature through an individual personalisation button. The reality is that on the Euro NCAP side we are trying to say that this is not a safety feature that is promoted. I am sure it continues to happen.

Professor Khastgir: We need to look into the root cause of why people do not want to use it or why they turn it off. The biggest reason is the distrust they have in these systems, and that distrust is caused by a number of things. First, they do not understand the system. Secondly, the system is providing false issues such as false positives, and it is getting you to turn when you do not want to turn, and as a result it is causing nuisance. We should not blame the driver for turning the system off; we need to look into the root cause of the reason behind it, which is distrust in the system.

How do we fix it? We need to ensure that we have higher performance standards for these systems. All these systems we are talking about that people turn off need to pass a set of five standard tests, and if they pass them that is all and you have it on your vehicle. In the real world it is a bit a bit more complex than five standard tests. If we can drive up the performance standards of these systems, that would lead to less nuisance from a usage perspective, and higher trust in these systems.

At WMG at University of Warwick we have done a lot of research into what leads to appropriate trust. We have coined this concept of informed safety, where we want to inform the driver of the capabilities but also the limitations of the system. What is happening right now is that the OEMs and the ecosystem are not informing people of the limitations. People will very much accept the limitations but they need to know; people do not like to be surprised. That is the change we need to bring in: not just publicise the capabilities but also inform the limitations, because the two together will lead to appropriate trust in the system.

Dr Arthur: That is a good point. The other half of this argument is that people are too confident in the system’s ability and become complacent. It is a matter of how we get the balance right so that people still pay attention when they are driving. We have all seen these videos of people driving along while reading books and all the rest of it.

Chair: We are not quite there yet but not far off.

Dr Arthur: We have been speaking about MOTs. I do not want to pre-empt things, but it seems quite likely that we might recommend that MOTs take more care in looking at these systems. Let us say that the day after I get my MOT I get my windscreen replaced because it gets chipped. If I do not go to a reputable provider, they may well just fit it and from my perspective it looks perfect but it is not quite right. How do we resolve that? How do we make sure that fitters are doing the right thing? If we assume we have fixed the MOT problem, how do we fix any work that has been done on the car between MOTs, or even in the first three years, because it is three years before the first MOT when a car is new?

Professor Cuerden: I feel I need to fact check. I agree with everything that everyone has said. The ADAS systems will be better if we have more trust in them, but remember that they are working and effective today on the road and are making a real difference. Siddartha talked really eloquently about how we can improve the performance standards so that they work for people. We wrote the original performance standard that was based on 2014-15 vehicle technologies and costs, which became regulation and went through the European Parliament in 2018-19.

It is catch-up time. I just wanted to make the point that we are in a good place, but if we join then we can make it even better. It is not just about the OEMs, the tier 1s and the supply chain that are going to put the kit on the vehicle; all that needs to catch up. We have standards in place—British standards, ISO and proper accountability through the supply chain—but it needs leadership.

Dr Arthur: Are there any penalties for someone who would fit my screen and not test it properly? Is there any comeback for me if somehow that results in an accident?

Ashley Patton: The honest answer is that I do not know. If you were to do it through your insurance company, it would do it through one of its approved and assured windscreen fitters. I do not know the market beyond that as the vehicles get older and people perhaps do not use their insurance companies. At the moment the cost through the insurance company is normally favourable, so most people will use the insurance company. Most of this is captured because of the economics, but there is a risk.

Stuart Lovett: What you have to remember is that the MOT testing stations reach a standard that is managed by DVSA. These are technicians who are there to maintain that standard, and they are doing that. The bigger issue here is that you could get an MOT failure and still drive away today, as people are doing.

More importantly, around 2.1 million people had an MOT tyre failure, yet 750,000 people still turned up the next year and got another MOT failure. They got an advisory for what we would argue is a safety-critical component, to say, “We advise you to take action.” TyreSafe would like to change it from an advisory to, “You need to take action.” People say, “Well, I got an advisory but I have 12 months to take action because it’s only an advisory.” It is quite shocking to think that 750,000 people turned up and the vehicle then failed on the second MOT. The engineers, technicians and garages are doing their jobs; it goes back to Siddartha’s point about people not listening.

Dr Arthur: Asking people to act on the advisory seems complicated. Is it not just better to increase the minimum depth of the tyre that is required on the vehicle? It keeps it nice and simple, doesn’t it?

Stuart Lovett: I will defer to my colleagues on that. As a charity, we are not asking for legislative change, just compliance with current legislation.

Chair: Can we pick up on the risks of ADAS? You have all touched on misunderstanding, misusing or disabling ADAS in various ways; how could the Government tackle those behaviour-type issues?

Professor Khastgir: I will provide you with three specific, tangible actions that the Government can take in order to do this. I would like to highlight that one action has already been taken by the Government from an automated vehicle perspective. A lot of the confusion right now is caused by people who believe that they are driving a self-driving, fully automated vehicle, when actually they are driving with a driver assistance system.

As per the UK Government’s Automated Vehicles Act 2024, we have now made it a criminal offence for any OEM or manufacturer to use specific words such as “self-driving” and “automated driving” for their driver assistance systems. We are the only country in the world that has done that, so we have already taken one action to avoid confusion.

The second point I wanted to make is that there is a lot of talk around novice and young drivers but not enough about education and raising awareness in schools. We talk about STEM engagement, inspiring the next generation into engineering and we go to schools, but we do not go to schools to get people more road-safety aware. I know for a fact there are other countries in the world that are consciously taking road safety to elementary and secondary schools. That is a very concrete action that we can take in order to tackle some challenges that we have with young and novice drivers.

The third point I want to make is about this concept of over-trust, which is actually much more dangerous than distrust. Over-trust leads to complacency in the system’s capabilities and leads drivers to use it in a way that the system is not designed to be used. To counter that we can and should come up with standards and regulations that prevent misuse from happening.

With my ISO hat on—sitting on various ISO standard committees and drafting some ISO standards—we are consciously making an effort to consider how we prevent misuse and what that entails as a requirement for the system. As engineers and policymakers, we have a responsibility to not just look into the system performance as it should be used but also to prevent misuse.

Samantha Dixon: I want to talk about the training of the professionals who fit Scott’s windscreen and do our MOTs. I acknowledge that this might be an enormous area that you may want to comment on, so I hesitate to ask the question, but are we training these professionals? Are they being trained properly?

Professor Cuerden: I do not know if they are being trained properly but we should be training more people. I am really interested in apprenticeships, and it reminds me of when I was younger and wanted to join this profession. We should be thinking about a national syllabus for this sort of thing. As Siddartha talks about, as more automation comes into play, who is going to look after those vehicles, service them and clean them, right through to the software management of cyber-security? It is quite complex but there is a programme there to take very seriously; otherwise, we will have to import it, which feels crazier.

Stuart Lovett: With regard to the training, I have no evidence to say that there is an issue there, and it is certainly not something that I would want to discuss, other than the fact we know there are a lot of vacancies in the MOT testing stations and industry. As Richard was saying, we need to have more people available, because there is obviously a wait. The biggest issue here, as Siddartha was saying, is that there is a complete lack of understanding from the general public and, alarmingly, also from business. They do not understand the importance of these systems so they switch them off. We know people do that because they are worried that it might cost them money at an MOT. These millions and millions of issues are being detected by the MOT stations but the public do not understand what they mean or what the potential risk is once they have an advisory.

One of the calls that we have made in our submissions to the Department for Transport and the THINK! team is that we strongly believe that a THINK! campaign around vehicle condition is important, and that there is a gap in the strategy. Of course, the response from DFT and THINK! is that the evidence is not there within STATS19, which massively under-reports the scale of this problem and does not even look at vehicle condition or the number of incidents, collisions or damage-only incidents. A THINK! campaign could raise awareness to the public of the importance; without that awareness, why would you take action?

Alex Mayer: I was thinking about whether the use of this kind of technology—having it both on and off—should be a part of driving tests. I was reminded of a friend of mine who said that the only reason they failed was because there was a branch in front of a 20 mph speed limit sign on the road and it had not flashed up on his dashboard. I thought, “Well, I know how to drive without that so I’m probably quite pleased that you failed your test on that.” There are certain things that can be switched on at the moment, but should there be a specific exercise on having them on and off and knowing how to use them?

Ashley Patton: The quick and easy answer is yes. As the technology becomes mandatory on vehicles it is really important that when you are learning to drive a vehicle you know how to drive it and all its functions.

Stuart Lovett: TyreSafe is already in discussions with DVSA—with the support of our partners—to ask for a potential change to the test, from a “tell me” to a “show me” question. We have the question: “Can you read the number plate from 20 metres away?” At the moment you can learn by rote. We know how to check the tread depth of a tyre by putting your finger in. We believe that if it was a “show me” question, the ADIs would have to show them how to do that, and then it would not just be a case of, “Well, I’ve learned it but I’ve never checked a tyre in my life.” Three out of five young drivers say they have never checked a tyre and would not know how to, but they have passed their driving test. That is a quick win that could be brought in: move from “tell me” to “show me”.

Ashley Patton: The only thing to add is that social media is an enormous problem, with misinformation on ADAS features and their capabilities. It would be great to have something as a single source of the actual truth.

Professor Khastgir: All I will say is that this is an increasingly serious issue for new technologies. For the existing technologies we have some level of control. The driving test should be updated for the new hands-off technologies that are coming right now with the new vehicles.

Alex Mayer: Richard, in October 2025 your research found that 97% of drivers are regularly or sometimes affected by headlight glare. Do we need to do any more research, or should we just get on with legislating?

Professor Cuerden: We need to do both. I appreciate that that is not a very helpful answer. We worked with the RAC on that study, which was done and paid for by the Department for Transport. Over half of the people surveyed said that they either did not or would not drive if they did not have to, because of glare, so we know it is a big issue out there.

The problem with glare is that although I understand how to measure the properties of light—luminance, intensity and brightness; I can do that quite well and I have teams of engineers who understand it well—I am struggling with the glare response in the human eye and linking it to those measures. If I change the parameters here, will I reduce glare? We do not yet understand the science. The things that contribute to glare are the road geometry, the LED type, the vehicle and the intensity. We can talk about the different headlights that dip and turn.

Unfortunately, as we age our eyes change, so we can get a lot more susceptible to the effect of glare, which is not necessarily linked to the thing I measure. On top of that, I mentioned earlier that a vehicle could be tested for MOT and go on the road and have headlights that are generating glare. It is through no fault of our MOT testers; it is just the way the test has been designed.

Chair: Am I right that the output of LED lights is not measured because it is not in legislation yet?

Professor Cuerden: Yes. I am going to struggle with some detail on this. The area the light falls on is measured, but the intensity of the light—the lux—and some other properties are specific to different light sources. The light regulations are being updated. We absolutely must contribute to the UN working groups and update the lighting standards for international vehicles. At the same time we must make sure that we are making the right changes. My concern is that we might find ourselves measuring something in a regulation that we can measure, but that may not have the outcome we intended of reduced glare.

Professor Khastgir: I want to add an important point. The issue of glare is not just a UK issue. We are aware that a lot of countries internationally are having the same issue. I would like to highlight Canada as one country that is championing a lot of the research and regulations in this space, to the extent that at the United Nations right now a glare taskforce has been created to tackle this issue. The UK has an opportunity here—through the work that Richard, colleagues and the Department for Transport have done—to demonstrate international collaboration and global leadership to directly update the regulations, not in terms of lighting in general but from a glare perspective.

Dr Arthur: A few months ago we had a debate in Westminster Hall about headlight glare, which was very enlightening. The Minister present mentioned the UN approach, and I am pretty sure he or she said that we would not see the benefit of a change until the early 2030s—2032 comes to mind. When is a vehicle that we can buy in a showroom first going to benefit from these changes?

Professor Khastgir: The challenge with dealing with regulations is that when you update a regulation you also update an enforcement date, and then it is only valid for new vehicles manufactured after that date. There is nothing we can do with that framework because that is the framework all the countries globally have adhered to.

To your point, you are articulating more towards what we do with the existing vehicles we have, or the vehicles that will get manufactured up until that day. Unfortunately, we do not have many tools in our library to tackle the vehicles that we already have, because they are adhering to today’s regulations. Unless we update the regulation there is nothing we can do. All we can do is educate and increase awareness among the general public about how to use the automatic dimming headlights, what type of headlights should be used and so on. We do not have the tools for existing vehicles that are being manufactured; we can only prevent future vehicles, to the best of my knowledge.

Dr Arthur: We are five years away from that change and probably another five years away from having a reasonable number of those vehicles on the road. It is a long time to fix a problem that, as we heard from Richard, can be quite debilitating for some people in terms of their ability to get out and about in their community. I am not blaming you, Siddartha.

Samantha Dixon: Siddartha, you mentioned the automatic dimming technology that we already have, which people may not be using because it is limited or they do not feel confident about it. What more do you think the Government could be doing to improve the driver’s use of this technology? Do you think it would help? Or are there other measures that we could be encouraging the Government to take forward?

Professor Khastgir: I would be repeating myself on this particular topic. It is essentially about getting the users to understand when to use it, when not to use it and what the benefits are of using automatic dimming headlights. A lot of people are not even aware there is an auto setting in the vehicle to enable the headlight configuration. There is a lot of awareness work that can be done at a dealership level or as part of awareness campaign aspects.

Samantha Dixon: I suppose it goes back to Ashley’s point about the single source of truth. This speaks to what Stuart in particular has been talking about. How far do vehicle defects contribute to road collisions? How effective is the current system at identifying and dealing with unsafe vehicles? We have touched on this already. Stuart, do you want to begin? I would also welcome comments from other panel members.

Stuart Lovett: We have to differentiate between trying to reduce road collisions. The strategy is talking about killed and seriously injured, which is taken from the STATS19. While it is arguably the best system in the world, it still has issues, because it is the policeman’s perception at the time. What we are trying to articulate is that we need to be looking beyond the STATS19.

Even if we use STATS19, what we are saying and have provided in the evidence is that while the strategy talks about the need to reduce 18,000 casualties by 2035, everything we have talked about is new technology and new systems that are coming, and it is going to take time, but we have to deliver the casualty savings now. In STATS19 we saw a rise in cases where the police identified a tyre-related defect that contributed to the collision—that has gone up 19% in one year—so we have broken 201 people in cases where the police deemed tyres to have been a contributory factor. From work that we have done in the past, when I was at National Highways looking at the police forensic fatal files, which TRL has analysed, the tyre was a cause in 75% of issues. In the work we did with TRL we were able to talk about causation rather than one of six contributory factors. In 75% of cases, the police forensic examiners determined that the fatality could have been avoided by better care and maintenance of that vehicle.

That is how we could start to drive down not only the number of incidents—you do not know where the next fatality is going to come; we must also prevent damage-only and collisions. We have had fatalities on the motorway because the primary incident was a breakdown or a tyre failure. If we look at addressing the bigger issue in the strategy and get the vehicle defects in the strategy, more attention will be focused on that.

Samantha Dixon: You mentioned the 201 fatalities last year—

Stuart Lovett: No, KSIs: killed or seriously injured.

Samantha Dixon: Do you think the Government understand the scale of that?

Stuart Lovett: Of course; this is DFT’s data analysis of the police. There is the usual response of, “Let’s focus just on KSIs,” but we do not know where the next one is coming from. What we are saying in our evidence that we presented to the Committee is that if we look at and introduce leading and lagging indicators based on what engineers in the testing stations are saying is a potential risk now and moving forward, we will start to see a reduction in the number of collisions and incidents, which must lead to a reduction in the number of KSIs. This can be delivered now or next year, not in 2030 or 2035. It could be delivered pretty quickly.

Jacob Collier: All the technology that we have talked about is great, but obviously it has to be working throughout the lifetime of the vehicle. How could the Government ensure that they collect that data to ensure that vehicles continue to have this technology working in the way that they should throughout the whole lifetime of the vehicle?

Professor Cuerden: I am going to repeat myself but I feel I have to. Remember that I talked about 14,000 killed and seriously injured? Over 1,000 people are not going to die and lots of people are going to be saved by this technology as it is today, with all the limitations we just discussed. We know that from the data we have today. It took my team an awful long time and a lot of energy and effort using Python code to do the modelling.

What we do not know in easy-to-find ways, which is crazy in the modern digital world, is about the kits, the vehicles and the mileage they are doing. Linking the datasets we have already and making that within all the right rules—I do not want to identify people, but making that available to academics and fellow researchers—is going to help us to understand. The next time somebody like me does a study and says what the benefits are going to be, it can be more peer-reviewed and looked at. We have the data; I just do not think we are co-ordinating how we get it, use it and make it available.

Stuart Lovett: We need to make sure that the technology is enabled on the vehicle at the MOT. People are switching it off because a warning light has come on and that would potentially result in an MOT failure. You either take the fuse out—we are hearing that anecdotally—or you switch it off if the capability is there.

If we look at the TPMS, which is in the strategy, the warning light only comes on if it is around about 20% under inflation, which will significantly affect the handling and stopping performance of the vehicle. But you can turn that off. What we need is the MOT testing stage to say, “The strategy is relying on this new technology; it has to be enabled, and if it is not enabled, why not?” If you have chosen to switch that off, maybe that should be either an advisory or a fail.

Ashley Patton: We also need to make sure that our accident statistic data and what we collect in terms of the state of the vehicle and any other wrap-around is essentially going to be fit for purpose for new technologies. For example, was the feature switched off? We need to make sure we are proactive in that.

Jacob Collier: Professor Siddartha, you said in your written evidence that you recommended a new way of monitoring ADAS performance for vehicles after they have been sold. Could you elaborate on that and any suggestions you think the Government should take up?

Professor Khastgir: The suggestion in the written evidence is inspired by what the Government and the wider ecosystem are already doing for automated driving. There is a concept in automated driving called in-service monitoring and reporting. This is a legal requirement for any vehicle that is fully automated, be it a robo-taxi or any other service. Whenever an incident happens, a full report and an investigation needs to be provided by the developer to the regulator.

In addition to that, a periodic report also needs to be provided to the regulator by the manufacturer and operator. A similar thing can also be done, especially for more advanced ADA systems where we get information and, very much aligned to what Ashley and Richard were saying, the data gets created on when and how many miles are being driven with the ADAS switched on and off. That is the fundamental thing that we could achieve from the data collection itself.

One more thing I wanted to add is that the Government can absolutely do something about taking steps to ensure that the day-zero performance of an ADA system is the same on day 100, day 1,000 and day 5,000. We do not currently have a mechanism to make that happen.

Chair: I have a question that I have thought of as a result of what we have covered. We have covered digital and physical safety issues around vehicles on the road at the moment, and we are thinking about what the Government could do, either legislatively or in other ways, in terms of recommendations that we might make for the Government’s road safety strategy. On the relationship between switching tech on or off, or the issues Stuart has covered, such as tyre safety, the majority of drivers take out insurance and are careful to make sure that their policy is up to date and accurate; could there be a role for insurance companies to incentivise drivers not to switch the kit off and so on? Are there some examples? I do not understand enough about the relationship between insurance companies and drivers in terms of incentives or disincentives in that respect.

Professor Cuerden: For many years now we have had telematics on vehicles, so we understand the new driver insurance product.

Chair: I am not talking about those specific products.

Professor Cuerden: Yes, but take that model. Imagine now the model is that you have in-vehicle data. In the traditional model you had a retrospective add-on to the vehicle. Now you have that data in the vehicle. We have helped the European Commission to design what data is stored, where it is stored and how it is accessible on the vehicle. That could be available to insurance companies through a cloud server, under an agreement. Therefore, if I am not getting speed warning alerts at a certain amount, I would pay less per mile. We will be seeing that sort of product.

Chair: So that interconnection of data is possible but not currently done?

Professor Cuerden: Yes. Imagine if an OEM wants to help to sell you the insurance; that is the way the market is going to go.

The other point I want to add quickly—Siddartha is going to come in and say much more intelligent things—is that part of the general safety regulations is event data recorders, which are a black box in your vehicle. We had a real problem taking this through the European Commission on a cost-benefit study, because what is the benefit of knowing what went wrong? I cannot put a monetary value to it. We got around that because we asked the manufacturers, “Who doesn’t collect the data?”, and everyone already collected it, so there was no cost and that is why it has gone in. If there is no cost and you get the benefit, you can learn from it.

If the worst happens now—in more advanced vehicles that are doing more of the driving for us or assisting us driving—we are going to know at the point of collision not just the speed, lights and whether you had your seatbelt on, but what systems you were using. As people get used to that and use their systems well, that will be really helpful. I am indemnifying myself because I was driving at the correct speed.

Stuart Lovett: I am afraid to say that TyreSafe has singularly failed to engage with the insurance industry, whether as a collective or with individual companies, despite all our requests. I am not hopeful that they would want to engage on this, but if so then it might require legislative change, or changes to their own policies and procedures, which again will be kicking the can down the road.

A quick win that could be enabled as soon as next year—we have tried to engage with DFT on this—is the very thing that we have been saying: explain to the public, the driver and the company, particularly if you are a company driver, why these systems are important and their potential risks and benefits. We can change behaviour much more quickly than perhaps we can introduce legislative or policy changes with various organisations.

The public do not understand these systems: “If you switch it off, it might save me the cost of replacing a light or something.” Explain it to them. If there is a potential risk of that being detected by the police when they are looking at whether you have had an MOT failure or advisory, and we know they can check these systems, or the road collision investigation branch looks at the MOT history and the fact that you have not taken action, that will then start making a behavioural change in this country on the importance of this issue.

From TyreSafe’s point of view, a national public campaign such as a THINK! campaign to explain the importance of the technology—about the roadworthiness of vehicles, how these systems are there to help you and what can compromise them—would be a quick win and very effective.

Professor Khastgir: One of the biggest benefits of these new technologies, apart from safety, is the data that they will generate, and the OEM or operator will have access to the data. The question is: how do they or somebody else in the ecosystem monetise or incentivise it? The frameworks do not exist as of now, but I am very sure that in time there will be models that will be created either by insurers or OEMs to incentivise it. The data will exist, which is a big benefit when we did not have the data 10 years back.

Chair: That brings us to the end of our first panel and what has been a really interesting session. Thank you for your evidence and for preparing for today. if there is anything you feel you want to add or that you did not have a chance to say today, please write in fairly soon so that we can include it in our report. I am going to suspend the meeting for a few moments while we change panels.
